title: Cold Lead
tagline: Every warm lead was a cold lead first; the label describes a stage, not a verdict.
excerpt: A prospect matching your ICP who hasn't engaged yet, the starting point of a sequence, not a dead end.
definition: A prospect matching your ICP who hasn't engaged with any outreach yet, the starting point of a sequence, not a signal that they won't ever respond.
body: A cold lead is where every outbound sequence starts: a person who fits your ideal customer profile but has never engaged with you. Cold describes the relationship, not the prospect's likelihood of buying. Treating a cold lead as a lost cause after one unanswered email is the most common way outbound teams undersell their own pipeline. Most replies come from the second, third or fourth touch in a sequence, not the first, which is exactly why a real cadence exists instead of a single email. Busy buyers miss messages, read them at the wrong moment or wait to see whether you follow up at all. Say a team emails 100 cold leads and hears back from 3 after the first message. If they stop there, they never find out how many of the other 97 would have replied to a sharper second or third touch. The quality of a cold lead depends on the list, not the label: a well-researched contact with a recent trigger, such as a new role or a funding round, is a far better cold lead than a name pulled from a broad database. Mark a cold lead as unresponsive only after a full sequence across more than one channel.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a cold lead and a warm lead?
faqs.answer: A cold lead fits your ideal customer profile but has never engaged with you; a warm lead has. Opening emails, accepting a connection or replying neutrally turns a cold lead warm. Both can become customers, but they need different handling: cold leads need a relevant first reason to talk, warm leads need nurturing.

faqs.question: How many times should you contact a cold lead?
faqs.answer: Usually four or five touches spread over two to three weeks, across email and LinkedIn where possible. Each touch should add something new, such as a different angle or a short proof point, rather than repeating the first message. After that, move the lead to a later sequence triggered by a new signal.

faqs.question: How do you warm up a cold lead?
faqs.answer: Show relevance before you ask for anything. Reference a real trigger, such as a new role, a hire or an expansion, engage with their LinkedIn posts, and make the first message about their likely problem rather than your product. A cold lead warms up when they recognise you as someone who understands their situation.
